Democrat party plans for the next couple years?

If memory serves, Howard Dean pushed for a 50-state strategy a decade ago or so. This meant that the Democrat party would commit resources to all 50 states no matter how unlikely it was that they would win certain races. This was also meant for local elections, not just the Presidency. Again if memory serves, they implemented this strategy for a few years and then abandoned it, after which things went downhill for them.

If the Democrats truly want to be a national party, they have to go back to the 50-state strategy.

There are a couple of benefits to the 50-state strategy. You are forced to think about the needs of your constituency in all 50 states, not just certain regions of the country. This will in-turn give you better insight into what people around the country actually think as compared to raw, unfeeling polling data. This will also temper the extremes of your party by trying to include various people from around the country under one tent and working towards common goals. Lastly, you force your opponent to have to commit resources in races that they might not otherwise have to do.

The Democrats probably won't re-visit the 50-state strategy though. It's not just a reluctance to admit their failings, it is also some other things:

  • The Democrats are sometimes too calculating for their own good (they relied on polls too much this go round, for instance). They look at spending money on long shot races in the south as a waste. They don't factor in the soft benefits of spending money on noncompetitive races. The irony is that Democrats are supposed to be the party of empathy where people share their stories and have their voices heard.

  • They still think they can rely on changing demographics to bring them widespread victories in the future.

  • The left wing echo chamber is much more deceptive than the right wing equivalent. The leftist viewpoint is the default template in academia, social media, movies, etc. This in turn deceives Democrats into thinking their viewpoint is more popular than it actually is (ergo no need to change).

Finally, the ground is shifting to where people think less in terms of left/right and more in terms of globalist/nationalist and authoritarian/libertarian. I think the people who voted Republican this time around are slightly ahead of the people who voted Democrat in this regard.
